problem_type: Where a saved API key is sent is decided by data (tool arguments, on-disk catalog rows, a declaration card) rather than by the user, and the only thing checking it sees just one of those sources
symptom: nomi_integration_manage action=update_vendor accepted baseUrl / authType / authHeader / authQueryParam for a connection that already held an encrypted key, patched the vendor row, and left the key in place. An unsigned piece of conversation text could therefore redirect the user's credential to another host, and the MCP surface advertised that capability in its published inputSchema (8 field occurrences across two tools on origin/main 1ba0c0cb5). nomi_integration begin took baseUrl the same way. Nothing in the repository failed because of this.
direct_cause: catalogManagement.manageModelCatalogConnection looped over a field list that included baseUrl and the three auth-placement fields and wrote them through upsertModelCatalogVendor, while the credential record for that vendor key was untouched.
class_root: Same-origin was enforced in exactly one place: validateProviderAdapterDraft, at the moment a declaration card is received. That layer can only see the card in its hand. It cannot see a vendor row written by an earlier version, a model-catalog.json edited by hand, a second write entrance added later, or a mapping whose create.path is an absolute URL to another host and was already on disk. The P2 self-check question — can the same problem come back from another caller, another version, another platform, or old data? — had no answer, so the invariant was not owned by any layer that every outbound request passes through. Cherry Studio states the same rule as an architectural constraint (unsigned data must never control credential destinations); none of the nine products surveyed lets an agent change the address of a connection that already holds a key.
affected_population: Every user who has ever saved a key for an HTTP provider: any signed MCP host could redirect that key by calling update_vendor
Every connection whose catalog row was written by an older build or edited by hand, where the address no longer matches what the user approved
Every custom-call script, which reaches vendorHttp with the user's key and had no destination owner at all (customCallRunner deliberately skips private-network filtering)
Every declaration card whose asset-upload initiate endpoint or self-check probe pointed at another host: both carry the key and neither was covered by the existing same-origin check
entry_points: External MCP host calling the model-onboarding tools
Renderer model-settings page saving or re-saving a key
Canvas generation submit and poll (every mapping-driven provider request)
Hand-written custom-call script executing against a vendor
Catalog import of a model-catalog package
invariants: Any outbound request carrying the user's key must have an origin equal to the origin the user confirmed and saved on the credential page, or an origin declared in compiled-in code (a provider's officially announced fallback domain)
The binding is written by exactly one transaction — the one that writes the key — and is never read from an upsert payload, so no data path can set it
Changing where a key is sent, or how it is placed, is possible only by going through the credential page again
No MCP tool's published inputSchema may contain baseUrl, baseUrlHint, authType, authHeader, authQueryParam, authScheme or proxyUrl
Absence of a binding is not a refusal: an old install, a curated seed or a local ComfyUI connection has none, and those fall back to the existing private-network policy
A refusal on this criterion happens before any byte leaves the machine, so the user is told nothing was charged
The binding stores no credential-bearing value: the proxy URL can carry user:pass, so only a boolean is recorded

door_reduction.why_not: Recounted during the #812/#817 integration with the same symbol identities on pre-merge main 0d8e4c87c5e97adf0c14d54f4fbd4c9d2340078e (28) and this branch (41). Targets: CredentialBinding, FAMILIES, ProviderAdapterDraft, VENDOR_CONFIG_FIELD_CLASSIFICATION, applyApiKeyUpsert, assertCardLevelOperations, authorizeSubmitDestination, bindCredentialDestination, codeDeclaredFallbackOrigins, credentialBinding, declaredAssetIngestionSchema, deriveCredentialBinding, joinUrl, readCredentialBinding, upsertModelCatalogVendor, validateProviderAdapterDraft. FAMILIES and VENDOR_CONFIG_FIELD_CLASSIFICATION identify actual reads in the fallback-origin and credential-field owners; declaration bindings themselves are not doors. The old 32/31 line-based counts are replaced, not carried across incompatible units. The increase includes new binding and declaration-card references; the legacy catalogManagement write entrance remains deleted. The rest are deliberately not merged, and the reason is the point of this fix: the five joinUrl call sites are five different request builders and merging them would mean one transport for mappings, custom-call scripts and the apimart provider — a rewrite of the generation core, not a fix. What was missing was never fewer doors but one layer that every one of them passes through, and that layer already existed: vendorHttp.requestVendor -> authorizeSubmitDestination is a single write door, and the new criterion lives inside that same function rather than in a second classifier (check:outbound-policy enforces exactly that). The three applyApiKeyUpsert call sites are the same function reached through upsertModelCatalogVendorApiKey and mutateCatalog().upsertApiKey; the binding is written inside it, so all three bind.

generality_proof: The criterion is evaluated on the final URL of every request that vendorHttp builds, for every vendor, with carriesCredential decided by collectRequestSecretValues — the same function that already computes which exact values in this request are secrets for redaction. It is therefore independent of which code built the request (mapping, custom-call script, asset upload, self-check), of which provider it is, and of whether the address came from a card, a seed, a hand edit or an older build.

shared_boundaries.responsibility: The single transport every provider request passes through, whatever built it: mapping, custom-call script, asset upload or self-check. The send-time half of the invariant is evaluated here, inside the existing authorizeSubmitDestination call, so it is not a second destination classifier.
The single transaction that writes a key. The bind-time half of the invariant is written here, so a binding cannot have a second write entrance.

The gate that keeps the two halves from drifting apart: it is the only thing that can see a new write entrance or a newly advertised destination field, neither of which any single runtime layer can observe.

same_class_entry_points.evidence: assertCardLevelOperations rejects an initiate endpoint on another origin; electron/providerAdapter/declarationCard.test.ts covers it with its same-origin positive control.
Same function asserts the probe path with assertSafePath against the provider base URL; declarationCard.test.ts covers the cross-origin probe.

same_class_entry_points.entry_point: Hand-written custom-call script issuing a vendor request
same_class_entry_points.evidence: It reaches vendorHttp.requestJson, so the send-time criterion applies to it unchanged; it had no destination owner at all before (the file comment states private-network filtering is deliberately skipped).

same_class_entry_points.entry_point: Second-step upload to a presigned URL returned by the provider
same_class_entry_points.evidence: That request carries no key by design (catalog/types.ts states the policy), so carriesCredential is false and the private-network policy judges it alone; credentialOriginBinding.test.ts has that positive control.

recurrence.reason: Three independent places let data decide the destination (begin's baseUrl, update_vendor's patch, and the design's connect_provider upsert), which is what a class root looks like rather than a slip. It will recur whenever a new write entrance for connection settings is added, because nothing but a gate can see that.
same_class_scan: node scripts/door-map.mjs applyApiKeyUpsert upsertModelCatalogVendor authorizeSubmitDestination joinUrl bindCredentialDestination

Enumerated every call site of upsertVendor / upsertModelCatalogVendor / applyVendorUpsert in electron/ and src/ and classified each as an owner or a violation (that enumeration is now the gate's rule 1)
Read every MCP tool's published inputSchema for the seven destination field names (that read is now the gate's rule 2, and it runs the real resolver rather than grepping source)

prevention.invariant: Only registered owners may write a destination field into a persisted vendor row; no published MCP inputSchema may contain one of the seven destination field names; and the outbound guard must still call judgeCredentialDestination and readCredentialBinding.
prevention.failure_mode: Each finding names the file and line (rule 1), the tool and the field (rule 2), or the missing call (rule 3), and the epilogue says the fix is not to add the file to the owner list but to answer which page the user saw this write on.
prevention.strategy: Owners are registered with a one-line reason of the form 'the user saw and approved this write on page X'; there is no numeric baseline to raise, so the only way to pass is to answer that question. Rule 1 parses the arguments of every upsert call rather than matching field names anywhere in the file, because the same names are request-building locals in dozens of places and a name-anywhere rule produced 211 findings and would have been switched off within a week. Rule 2 runs MCP_TOOL_RESOLVER so a schema derived from declarations is covered exactly like a hand-written one. Rule 3 matches the calls, not the string 'credentialBinding', because renaming the symbol keeps the substring while stopping the check.

legacy_paths.rationale: The update_vendor write path was the violation itself, so it is deleted rather than guarded; the two hand-written MCP tools that advertised the destination fields went with the tool-face replacement in the same series. Installs that saved a key before this change simply have no binding: they are not refused, the criterion does not apply, and the existing private-network policy judges them alone until the user next saves that key.

migration: None. Vendor.credentialBinding is a new optional top-level field; absent means no binding, which is the pre-existing behaviour. applyVendorUpsert inherits it from the existing row so an ordinary settings edit cannot clear it.
residual_risks: A user who genuinely changes a provider's endpoint must re-save the key. That is the intended cost and it is stated in the refusal message, but it is a real extra step and was not walked through with a real user in this batch.

The binding records the origin only. A provider that legitimately serves one API from several origins without announcing them in vendorBaseFallback would be refused until the user re-saves; no such provider is known in the current catalog, and the refusal names both origins so the cause is visible.

No paid live generation was run against a rebound connection in this batch. The criterion is covered by unit tests plus one end-to-end test that proves the request never leaves the machine; a real provider call on a real rebinding is handed to the verification lane.

Plan finding 10 / Q11 claimed a LAN user cannot see the destination on the paste-key page. Measured on 2026-09-18 it is the other way round: the page that actually takes the key renders descriptor.display.baseUrl straight from the session config with no private-network stripping, so http://192.168.1.20:8000/v1 is shown in full (credentialPageShowsDestination.test.ts renders the real page and asserts it). What safeHandoffOrigin strips is a different payload — the handoff hint that brings the Nomi GUI forward — and that stripping is load-bearing: handoffQueue.normalizeDisplayOrigin throws 'Private handoff origin requires authorization' on a private origin by design, so removing it would stop a local ComfyUI or LAN relay from opening the credential page at all. The residual risk is therefore not the one the plan named; it is that the GUI settings panel reached through that hint shows no origin for private targets, which is a second boundary (the handoff queue's own security decision) and is deliberately left untouched here.

applyVendorUpsert rebuilds the vendor row from an explicit field list, so any Vendor field not named there is silently dropped by an ordinary upsert — assetIngestion is already one of them. This fix only patched credentialBinding into that list (inherited from the existing row, never read from the payload), which is a per-field patch, not a cure. It is known, reported, and scheduled as its own separate change; the structural repair is to make the rebuild a whitelist-overwrite rather than a whitelist-preserve.

invariant_owner_layer.rationale: The invariant has two halves and neither layer can hold both, so the owner is named as the send-time layer (electron/vendor/vendorOutboundGuard.ts) with electron/catalog/catalogStore.ts applyApiKeyUpsert as its bind-time counterpart, listed in shared_boundaries. Bind time is the only moment the user's confirmation exists, and the key write is the single transaction that owns it. Send time is the only layer every request passes through regardless of who built it, which is what makes the criterion survive old data and future write entrances. It is deliberately not owned by validateProviderAdapterDraft: that layer is where the problem is discovered on a fresh card, not where it is prevented.

internal_only_reason: Not internal-only: the refusal is user-visible, carries its own error code and has zh/en copy in generationCommon.

dependency_lifecycle.rationale: No dependency is added, upgraded or retained: everything here is first-party — one catalog module, one criterion inside the existing outbound guard, and one gate script.
